title: What Is Misinformation?
summary: Learn the difference between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation, and why false stories spread so fast.
content: Misinformation is false or misleading information shared by someone who believes it is true. They are not trying to trick anyone.
Disinformation is false information created or spread on purpose to deceive people, often for money, attention, or political influence.
Malinformation is real information used to cause harm, such as leaking someone's private details or sharing a true fact out of context to hurt someone.
False stories often spread faster than true ones because they are surprising, emotional, and easy to share without reading.
tips: Strong emotion (anger, fear, excitement) is a signal to slow down
Ask: who benefits if I believe this?
Sharing something false by accident still spreads harm

questions.prompt: Your aunt forwards a post saying drinking hot water every hour cures the flu. She truly believes it and wants to help her family. What is this?

options.text: Misinformation
Disinformation
Malinformation
Satire

questions.explanation: The claim is false, but your aunt is sharing it because she believes it. False + no intent to deceive = misinformation.

questions.prompt: A group creates a made-up story about a city mayor and posts it from 50 fake accounts at the same time. What is this?

options.text: Misinformation
Disinformation
Malinformation
Breaking news

questions.explanation: The story is invented and spread on purpose using fake accounts. Deliberate deception = disinformation.

questions.prompt: True or false: If a post has been shared by thousands of people, it is probably true.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Popularity is not proof. False posts often get shared more because they are shocking or emotional.

title: Clickbait
summary: Learn why some headlines are designed to make you click, not to inform you.
content: Clickbait headlines use curiosity, shock, or strong emotion to get clicks.
They often hide the key fact so you have to open the article to find out what happened.
Clickbait is not always completely false, but it usually exaggerates or misleads, and the article often does not deliver what the headline promised.
tips: ALL CAPS or many exclamation marks
'You won't believe...' or 'What happened next...' phrasing
No specific facts in the headline

questions.prompt: Which headline is more likely to be clickbait?

options.text: City council approves $2M budget for road repairs
You WON'T BELIEVE what the city just did with YOUR money!!!

questions.explanation: Option B hides the actual fact and uses caps and emotional language to bait a click. Option A tells you exactly what happened.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest sign of a clickbait headline?

options.text: It names the place where the event happened
It hides the main fact to make you curious
It includes a number, like a date or amount
It is written in plain, calm language

questions.explanation: Clickbait works by creating a 'curiosity gap': it withholds the key fact so you feel you must click.

questions.prompt: True or false: A clickbait headline is always completely false.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Clickbait can be technically true but exaggerated or misleading. The problem is manipulation, not always outright lies.

title: Fake Headlines
summary: Spot made-up headlines that are designed to look like real news.
content: Fake headlines copy the style of real news so they look believable at a glance.
Watch for look-alike web addresses, such as a real outlet's name with an extra word or an unusual ending like '.news-alerts.co'.
Real major news is usually reported by several trusted outlets. If only one unknown site has the story, be careful.
Fake headlines often sound overly certain ('PROVES', 'CONFIRMED', 'EXPOSED') and leave out details like names, dates, or sources.
tips: Check the web address carefully
Search whether other trusted outlets report the same story
Be suspicious of absolute words like 'PROVES' or 'ALWAYS'

questions.prompt: Which headline is more trustworthy?

options.text: Scientists PROVE coffee makes you live forever
Study of 10,000 adults links moderate coffee intake to slightly lower heart risk

questions.explanation: Option B gives specific, measured details and avoids exaggeration. Option A makes an impossible, absolute claim.

questions.prompt: You see 'BREAKING: All state universities closing tomorrow' on a site called rivertonherald.news-alerts.co. What should you do first?

options.text: Share it right away to warn your friends
Check your university's official website and other news outlets
Read the comments to see if people believe it
Trust it because it says 'BREAKING'

questions.explanation: Go to the official source. The odd web address and dramatic claim are red flags, and a real closure would be on the university's own site.

questions.prompt: Which headline is more trustworthy?

options.text: Riverton Public Library extends weekend hours starting March 1, city announces
Government HIDING the truth about library closures - share before it's deleted!

questions.explanation: Option A names who announced it and when. Option B uses fear, urgency, and no evidence.

title: Manipulated Images
summary: Learn how photos can be edited, AI-generated, or taken out of context to mislead you.
content: Images can mislead in three main ways: they can be edited, fully generated by AI (including deepfakes), or real photos shared with a false caption.
Out-of-context photos are the most common trick: a real photo from years ago or another country is shared as if it shows today's event.
Clues of editing or AI generation include strange shadows or lighting, warped backgrounds, extra or missing fingers, and blurry or nonsense text on signs.
A reverse image search (for example, Google Lens or TinEye) can show where and when a photo first appeared online.
tips: Look closely at hands, text, shadows, and reflections
Use reverse image search to find the original
A real photo can still have a fake caption

questions.prompt: A viral photo claims to show a shark swimming on a flooded highway after yesterday's storm. A reverse image search shows the same photo was posted in 2017 about a different storm. What is the problem?

options.text: Nothing, the photo is real
It is an old photo shared out of context
It is definitely AI-generated
It is satire

questions.explanation: Even if the photo is not edited, using a 2017 image to describe yesterday's storm is misleading. That is an out-of-context image.

questions.prompt: Which detail most strongly suggests a photo of a crowd was generated by AI?

options.text: The photo is a little blurry
Some people have extra fingers and the signs have warped, unreadable text
The colors are very bright
It was taken at night

questions.explanation: AI image tools often struggle with hands and text. Blurriness, bright colors, or night lighting happen in real photos too.

questions.prompt: True or false: If a photo has not been edited, the caption attached to it must be accurate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A completely real photo can be paired with a false caption about where, when, or what it shows.

title: Unreliable Sources
summary: Figure out whether a website or account is a source you can trust.
content: Trustworthy sources usually have a clear 'About' page, contact information, named writers, and a policy for correcting mistakes.
Warning signs include no named authors, lots of pop-up ads, emotional language everywhere, and no links to evidence.
Some sites are satire on purpose. Their stories are jokes, but screenshots of them often get shared as real news.
Fact-checkers use 'lateral reading': instead of judging a site by how it looks, they open new tabs and search what other trusted sources say about it.
tips: Look for an About page and named authors
Read laterally: search the source's name in a new tab
A professional design does not mean a reliable source

questions.prompt: You want to check a claim about a new vaccine study. Which source is most reliable?

options.text: An anonymous blog called 'TruthSeeker365'
The published study itself or an official public health agency
A viral video from a lifestyle influencer
A comment in an online forum

questions.explanation: Go to the original research or an official health agency. The others are second-hand and have no accountability.

questions.prompt: What does 'lateral reading' mean?

options.text: Reading the whole article slowly from top to bottom
Leaving the site and searching what other trusted sources say about it
Reading only the headline and the first paragraph
Reading the comments under the article

questions.explanation: Lateral reading means checking a source from the outside, in other tabs, instead of trusting what the site says about itself.

questions.prompt: True or false: A website with a professional, modern design is a trustworthy source.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Anyone can build a polished website cheaply. Design tells you nothing about accuracy.

title: Checking Authors
summary: Learn how to check who wrote something and whether they are qualified to write it.
content: Before trusting an article, check who wrote it. Is there a real, named author?
Look at whether the author's expertise matches the topic. A doctor writing about medicine is more relevant than a doctor writing about car engines.
Search the author's name. Do they have other published work? Are they a real person?
Watch for conflicts of interest: an author who sells a product may not be neutral when writing about it.
tips: Search the author's name in a new tab
Check that their expertise fits the topic
Ask: does the author make money if I believe this?

questions.prompt: An article about climate science is written by 'Dr. Max Steel'. His bio lists no university, and a search shows he sells 'climate detox' supplements. What is the main concern?

options.text: His name sounds unusual
His credentials cannot be verified and he has a conflict of interest
The article is too short
There is no concern

questions.explanation: Unverifiable credentials plus a product to sell are two big red flags about this author.

questions.prompt: Which author is most credible for an article about nutrition?

options.text: Registered dietitian, 12 years at Riverton Hospital, published in nutrition journals
Wellness enthusiast and lifestyle influencer
Anonymous staff writer
Famous actor who follows a special diet

questions.explanation: Option A has relevant training, real experience, and published work you can check.

questions.prompt: True or false: An article with no author named should be trusted less until you can confirm the information somewhere else.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Without an author, nobody is accountable for the content. Confirm it with another trusted source first.

title: Checking Dates
summary: Avoid being fooled by old news shared as if it happened today.
content: Old stories often come back online and get shared as if they are new. This is sometimes called 'zombie news'.
Always check the publish date (and update date) on an article, usually near the headline or at the bottom.
Screenshots usually cut off the date, so a screenshot alone can't tell you when something was published.
Even an accurate old story can mislead today, because situations, rules, and facts change over time.
tips: Find the publish date before sharing
Be careful with screenshots: they hide dates
Ask: is this still true today?

questions.prompt: A friend shares 'Huge storm cancels all flights at Riverton Airport!' The article link is dated 2019. What is the best response?

options.text: Cancel your own flight right away
Point out that the article is old and check the airport's current status
Share it with more people
Ignore the date because the story is real

questions.explanation: The story may have been true in 2019, but it says nothing about today. Check the current, official source.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to find when an article was really published?

options.text: The time your friend shared it on social media
The publish date on the article itself
The number of likes it has
Today's date

questions.explanation: When someone shared a story is not when it was published. Check the date on the original article.

questions.prompt: True or false: A screenshot of an article always shows when it was first published.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Screenshots often crop out the date, and they can be edited. Find the original article.

title: Fact-Checking
summary: Use simple, practical steps to check whether a claim is true.
content: A simple method for checking claims is SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims back to the original context.
Stop: if a post makes you feel a strong emotion, pause before you react or share.
Find better coverage: see whether trusted outlets or professional fact-checkers (such as Snopes, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, or AP Fact Check) have covered it.
Trace claims: find the original study, quote, or photo. Claims often change as they are passed along.
tips: Remember SIFT: Stop, Investigate, Find, Trace
Go back to the original source
Use reverse image search for photos

questions.prompt: A post makes you really angry and you want to share it right away. Using SIFT, what should you do first?

options.text: Stop and pause before reacting
Share it quickly before it disappears
Write an angry comment
Send it to a group chat

questions.explanation: The first step of SIFT is Stop. Strong emotions make us share without checking.

questions.prompt: A post says a 'study' shows chocolate improves exam scores by 50%. What is the best way to check it?

options.text: Trust it because it mentions a study
Trace it to the original study and read what it actually found
Count how many people liked the post
Ask a friend who likes chocolate

questions.explanation: Claims about studies are often exaggerated. The original study may have found something much smaller, or nothing at all.

questions.prompt: Which tool is best for checking whether a photo appeared online earlier?

options.text: A spell checker
Reverse image search
A VPN
Taking a screenshot

questions.explanation: Reverse image search finds earlier copies of a photo and shows where and when it first appeared.

title: Social Media Misinformation
summary: Understand how false content spreads on social media and how to respond.
content: Social media feeds often show posts that get the most reactions, and shocking or angry posts get a lot of reactions, true or not.
Bots and fake accounts can make a claim look more popular than it really is.
Urgent phrases like 'SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS' are designed to make you skip checking.
Screenshots of posts can be faked easily, and a verified badge only shows identity or a paid subscription, not accuracy.
You can help: do not share unverified posts, report false content, and correct friends kindly with a reliable source.
tips: Urgency is a red flag
Check the account's age and posting history
Correct kindly and include a source

questions.prompt: A post from a 2-day-old account says 'SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!! Doctors don't want you to know...' and has 40,000 shares. What should you do?

options.text: Share it, because 40,000 people can't be wrong
Don't share it; look for reliable sources and report it if it is false
Comment asking if it's true
Screenshot it and post it yourself

questions.explanation: A brand-new account, urgent language, and a 'secret' claim are classic red flags. Share counts can be boosted by bots.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest sign that an account might be a bot?

options.text: It posts photos of pets
It posts hundreds of times a day, has no profile photo, and a username with random numbers
It follows news accounts
It has a few hundred followers

questions.explanation: Very high posting volume, no personal details, and auto-generated usernames are common bot patterns.

questions.prompt: True or false: A verified badge proves that everything the account posts is accurate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A badge may confirm identity or a paid subscription. It says nothing about whether the posts are true.

title: Final Challenge: Can You Spot the Fake?
summary: Put everything together. Use all your skills to separate real from fake.
content: This is the final challenge. Each question mixes skills from earlier lessons: headlines, images, sources, authors, dates, and social media.
Before you answer, run through your checklist: Who made this? When? What is the evidence? What do other trusted sources say?
tips: Use SIFT on every question
Look for the red flags you've learned
Take your time; checking beats guessing

questions.prompt: Which headline is more trustworthy?

options.text: Riverton school board votes 5-2 to start classes 30 minutes later next fall
SHOCKING: Schools are secretly making kids sleep less, experts FURIOUS

questions.explanation: Option A gives a specific vote, a group, and a date. Option B uses shock words, vague 'experts', and no facts.

questions.prompt: A photo shows a famous landmark covered in snow, captioned 'Freak blizzard this morning!' It's summer, and a reverse image search finds the photo from a winter 5 years ago. What is it?

options.text: Real breaking news
An old photo shared out of context
A weather forecast
A trustworthy source

questions.explanation: The photo is real but from 5 years ago. Pairing it with 'this morning' makes it misleading.

questions.prompt: True or false: If several trusted news outlets independently report the same story, it is more likely to be accurate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Independent confirmation from multiple reliable sources is one of the best signs a story is accurate.

questions.prompt: A website called 'HealthTruthNow' claims a herbal tea cures diabetes. There is no author, no About page, and every article links to a shop selling the tea. What is the biggest problem?

options.text: The website has too many articles
No accountability plus a clear money motive
The tea might taste bad
There is no problem

questions.explanation: No author or About page means no accountability, and the site profits if you believe the claim.

questions.prompt: Your group chat shares a screenshot: 'Campus closed Friday due to gas leak!' There's no link and no date. What should you do?

options.text: Stay home Friday
Check the university's official website, email, or alert system
Forward it to more group chats
Trust it because your friends shared it

questions.explanation: A screenshot with no link or date can't be verified. Real campus closures come through official channels.

questions.prompt: Last one! Which post is more trustworthy?

options.text: Anonymous account: 'My cousin's friend says the water supply is POISONED. Spread the word!!'
City Water Department: 'Routine testing completed Oct 3. Results meet all safety standards. Full report linked.'

questions.explanation: Option B comes from the responsible official source, includes a date, and links evidence. Option A is a second-hand rumor with urgent language.
